lead: A random process is a family of random signals indexed by time. One outcome gives one waveform; the ensemble gives all possible waveforms. Communication noise, fading and speech are modelled this way. For a wide-sense stationary process the mean is constant and the autocorrelation depends only on the time gap τ. The Fourier transform of that autocorrelation is the power spectral density (PSD), which shows how average power is spread over frequency. This chapter builds these tools and applies them to a linear filter, where output PSD is |H(f)|² times input PSD.
prereq: You need expectation and distributions from Chapter 1.4 and the Fourier transform from Chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: A random process X(t) assigns a random variable to every time t. Fix one outcome in the sample space and you get a sample function x(t), also called a realization. Fix t and you get a random variable X(t). The ensemble is the set of all sample functions.
The mean is μ<sub>X</sub>(t)=E[X(t)]. The variance is σ<sub>X</sub>²(t)=E[(X(t)−μ<sub>X</sub>(t))²]. The autocorrelation compares values at two times:

blocks.where: E[·] is expectation; X(t<sub>1</sub>) and X(t<sub>2</sub>) are random variables at times t<sub>1</sub> and t<sub>2</sub>; R<sub>X</sub> has units of power if X is a voltage across 1 Ω.

blocks.text: The autocovariance removes the mean: C<sub>X</sub>(t<sub>1</sub>,t<sub>2</sub>)=R<sub>X</sub>(t<sub>1</sub>,t<sub>2</sub>)−μ<sub>X</sub>(t<sub>1</sub>)μ<sub>X</sub>(t<sub>2</sub>). When the mean is zero, autocorrelation and autocovariance are the same.

items: R<sub>X</sub>(0,0)=E[X²(t)] is average power at time t.
If the mean is zero, C<sub>X</sub>(0,0) equals the variance.

blocks.text: For two processes X(t) and Y(t), the cross-correlation is R<sub>XY</sub>(t<sub>1</sub>,t<sub>2</sub>)=E[X(t<sub>1</sub>)Y(t<sub>2</sub>)]. It measures how one signal follows another at a delay. In general R<sub>XY</sub>(τ) is not the same as R<sub>YX</sub>(τ). The standard relation is R<sub>XY</sub>(τ)=R<sub>YX</sub>(−τ). They are equal only in special cases.

Strict-sense stationary means every joint distribution depends only on time differences, not on absolute time. This is hard to prove. Wide-sense stationary (WSS) keeps only the first two moments fixed. A process is WSS when μ<sub>X</sub>(t)=μ<sub>X</sub> (constant) and R<sub>X</sub>(t<sub>1</sub>,t<sub>2</sub>)=R<sub>X</sub>(τ) with τ=t<sub>1</sub>−t<sub>2</sub>.

blocks.where: τ is the time gap in seconds; R<sub>X</sub>(τ) is the autocorrelation of a WSS process; the mean μ<sub>X</sub> is constant.

blocks.text: Ergodicity means a long time average of one sample function equals the ensemble average. Then you can measure μ<sub>X</sub> and R<sub>X</sub>(τ) from one recorded waveform. WSS does not imply ergodicity. A process with a random DC level is WSS but not ergodic in the mean.

For WSS, R<sub>X</sub>(τ) has three useful facts: R<sub>X</sub>(0)=E[X²]=average power; R<sub>X</sub>(−τ)=R<sub>X</sub>(τ) for real X; and |R<sub>X</sub>(τ)|≤R<sub>X</sub>(0). The last fact says no delay gives more correlation than zero delay.

A stationary random signal is a power signal, not an energy signal, so the ordinary Fourier transform of the process does not exist. Its average power in frequency is therefore described by the power spectral density S<sub>X</sub>(f). The Wiener–Khinchine theorem links it to autocorrelation:

blocks.where: f is frequency in hertz; τ is time delay in seconds; S<sub>X</sub>(f) is two-sided PSD in W/Hz; R<sub>X</sub>(τ) is in watts.

blocks.text: The inverse relation is R<sub>X</sub>(τ)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>S<sub>X</sub>(f)e<sup>j2πfτ</sup>df. Average power is the area under PSD: P=R<sub>X</sub>(0)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>S<sub>X</sub>(f)df. For a real process S<sub>X</sub>(f) is real, nonnegative and even: S<sub>X</sub>(−f)=S<sub>X</sub>(f). Some syllabi call it the power density spectrum. A one-sided PSD folds negative frequencies onto positive frequencies, so it is twice the two-sided value for f>0.
Pass X(t) through a linear time-invariant filter with frequency response H(f). The output Y(t) is WSS if X(t) is WSS. Its PSD is

blocks.where: H(f) is filter frequency response; |H(f)|² is power gain; S<sub>X</sub>(f) is input PSD; S<sub>Y</sub>(f) is output PSD in W/Hz.

blocks.text: The output mean is μ<sub>Y</sub>=H(0)μ<sub>X</sub>. Output average power is P<sub>Y</sub>=∫S<sub>Y</sub>(f)df=R<sub>Y</sub>(0). For an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth B hertz, H(f)=1 for |f|≤B and 0 elsewhere. White noise of two-sided PSD N<sub>0</sub>/2 then gives P<sub>Y</sub>=(N<sub>0</sub>/2)(2B)=N<sub>0</sub>B.

figure.caption: The rectangle is the two-sided PSD in the worked example: height 1 µW/Hz from −10 kHz to 10 kHz, with area 20 mW. The curve is R<sub>X</sub>(τ), which peaks at 20 mW at τ=0 and first reaches zero at τ=1/(2B), that is τB=0.5.

spec.aria: A rectangular PSD of height 1 microwatt per hertz between normalized frequency minus one and one, and an autocorrelation curve peaking at 20 milliwatts at zero delay and first crossing zero at normalized delay 0.5.

examples.question: White noise has two-sided PSD N<sub>0</sub>/2 = 10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz, so N<sub>0</sub> = 2×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz. It passes through an ideal low-pass filter with bandwidth B = 10 kHz and unit gain in the passband. Find the output average power and the output PSD height inside the passband.
steps: Input PSD: S<sub>X</sub>(f)=N<sub>0</sub>/2=1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz for all f.
Filter power gain: |H(f)|²=1 for |f|≤10 kHz, and 0 outside.
Output PSD: S<sub>Y</sub>(f)=|H(f)|²S<sub>X</sub>(f)=1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz inside ±10 kHz, and 0 outside.
Check with N<sub>0</sub>B: P<sub>Y</sub>=(2×10<sup>−6</sup>)(10<sup>4</sup>)=0.02 W. The PSD height stays 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz.
examples.answer: The output average power is 0.02 W (20 mW). The output PSD is 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz inside ±10 kHz and zero outside.
examples.check:
N0 = 2e-6
B = 10e3
S = N0 / 2
P = N0 * B
print(P)
print(S)
examples.output: PY = 0.02 W (20 mW); SY(f) inside the passband = 1×10−6 W/Hz

traps: R<sub>X</sub>(0) is average power E[X²], not variance. Variance is R<sub>X</sub>(0)−μ<sub>X</sub>². Only zero-mean processes make them equal.
Two-sided PSD integrates from −∞ to ∞. One-sided PSD integrates from 0 to ∞ and is twice as tall at positive frequencies. Mixing the two halves or doubles the answer.
WSS fixes only mean and autocorrelation. Strict stationarity fixes all joint distributions. WSS does not imply strict stationarity, except for Gaussian processes.
The output PSD uses |H(f)|², not H(f). A filter with voltage gain 2 gives power gain 4.
A random process has no ordinary Fourier transform. Do not write S<sub>X</sub>(f)=|F{X(t)}|² for one realization; use the autocorrelation transform.

quiz.a: A process whose mean is constant and whose autocorrelation depends only on the time difference τ.

quiz.q: Why is S<sub>X</sub>(f) nonnegative and even for a real WSS process?
quiz.a: It is the Fourier transform of an even autocorrelation and represents power density, so it cannot be negative; the even autocorrelation makes the transform real and even.

quiz.q: White noise with N<sub>0</sub>/2=2×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz passes an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth 5 kHz. Find the output power.
A WSS process has mean 2 V and R<sub>X</sub>(0)=13 W. Find average power and variance.
quiz.a: Average power is R<sub>X</sub>(0)=13 W. Variance is 13−2²=9 W.

quiz.q: A filter has H(f)=1/(1+jf/f<sub>0</sub>) and input PSD S<sub>X</sub>(f). Write the output PSD and output power.
Explain why a random DC level is WSS but not ergodic in the mean.
quiz.a: Its mean is constant and autocorrelation depends only on τ, so it is WSS. A single realization keeps one DC value forever, so its time average does not equal the ensemble mean.

quiz.q: State the Wiener–Khinchine theorem and give one use.
quiz.a: The PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation. It lets us find average power in a band by integrating S<sub>X</sub>(f).

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice PSD is estimated from finite records using Welch's method, which averages periodograms. Cyclostationary processes model signals whose statistics vary periodically, as in digital modulation. Modern wireless systems use these ideas in OFDM spectrum shaping and cognitive radio. Search "Welch PSD estimation" and "cyclostationary signal processing" to go further.
